justification: These ranges describe what a typical low-stakes heads-up limit opponent holds after each preflop line, before we have watched them play. With only two players the blinds come round every hand, so both seats play far more hands than at a full table. The button raises about half its hands and limps a good share of the weaker ones instead of folding them. The big blind, by contrast, gives up too often: it defends a raise with a little over half its hands, calling with most of them and re-raising only its better pairs and aces. Re-raises and caps are kept for clearly strong holdings. After the flop the narrowing rule trims each starting range street by street from what the player does.

ranges.justification: When the button only completes, the heads-up big blind checks with everything it did not want to raise, which is nearly the whole deck apart from its better pairs and big cards.

ranges.justification: A heads-up button that just completes the small blind usually holds a weak king, queen or jack, or a low suited hand it finds too pretty to throw away but too poor to raise.

ranges.justification: Raising first on the heads-up button covers about half of all hands: every pair, every ace, most kings and the better queens, jacks and connected cards that play well in position.
A big blind that raises after the button only completes has a hand worth building the pot with: a middle or high pair, a good ace, or two strong broadway cards.

ranges.justification: When the button limps and then only calls the big blind's raise, it is holding one of its weaker completing hands that it now feels priced in to see a flop with.

ranges.justification: Facing a button raise, a typical big blind flat calls with small and middle pairs, most aces and kings, and the connected or suited cards that can hit a flop hard.

ranges.justification: A button that limps and then re-raises the big blind is setting a trap, so it holds a premium pair of tens or better, or ace with queen or king.
The big blind re-raising a button open in a heads-up game shows a pair of sevens or more, a strong ace, or the best king and queen combinations.
After opening and getting re-raised by the big blind, the button keeps calling with its pairs, its better aces and the stronger kings, queens and suited connectors.

ranges.justification: If the big blind raised a limp and the button then re-raised, the big blind calls with medium pairs and the good broadway hands rather than folding them.

ranges.justification: Capping the betting from the heads-up button means jacks or better, ace with king, or a suited ace with queen; anything weaker would simply call the re-raise.
When the big blind puts in the final raise before the flop against a heads-up button, it almost always holds queens, kings, aces or ace with king.
